title: Catherine and the pope
hookLine: a young laywoman writes to the pope in Avignon and urges him back to Rome
carry: if you are what you should be

cards: The pope doesn't live in Rome. For a long stretch of years, the popes have lived in Avignon, in the south of France, in a great palace far from the city of Peter and Paul.
In Italy, a young woman from Siena, a wool dyer's daughter, has decided this is wrong. She holds no office and has no title.
She isn't a nun in a convent; she lives a life of prayer and service as a laywoman, one of Dominic's lay sisters, in her family's house.
And she starts writing letters: to princes, to cardinals, and to the pope himself, telling him, warmly and without flinching, to come home.

teach.b: Catherine of Siena couldn't easily write, the old accounts say, so she dictated. Her letters went out in Italian, the language she spoke, and they're still read today. They're bold.
She calls the pope by a tender family word, something like dear father, and in the same letter tells him plainly to be brave, stop hesitating, and return to Rome.
She doesn't flatter him or insult him. She speaks as one Christian to another who happens to hold enormous power, and reminds him what that power is for.
She went further than letters: she traveled to Avignon and spoke with him there. And the pope did return to Rome.
How much of that was Catherine's doing, historians weigh differently, and the return didn't end the church's troubles; a painful split came soon after.
Today the Catholic Church honors her as a saint and a Doctor of the Church.

teach.h: SET THE WHOLE WORLD ON FIRE.
teach.b: A saying handed down under her name is usually given in English like this: if you are what you should be, you will set the whole world on fire. It isn't about being impressive.

It's about being true to what you were made for. Jesus says something with the same heat in Luke, in the King James Bible: "I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled?"
In these letters, Catherine's fire was ink, and honesty, and love that wouldn't stay quiet in front of power.

how: Catholics honor Catherine of Siena as a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and her letters and her book, the Dialogue, are still read; some Christians who speak up to leaders in church and state look to her example.

games.q: you're Catherine. you believe the pope belongs in Rome, but he's far away in Avignon, and you hold no office at all. what do you do?
o: keep quiet; it isn't your place.
write to him, warmly and plainly, and then go to see him.
write angry letters to everyone who will listen.
games.why: she called him by a tender family word and told him to be brave and come home. then she traveled to Avignon herself.

practice: Think of someone who holds power over something you care about, a local official, a manager, a landlord.
In your head, find the first honest sentence you'd write them, the way Catherine might: warm, respectful, clear about what needs to change, with no insults and no flattery.
If you pray, ask for courage and the right words; if not, let the sentence settle until it sounds like you.

wordCard.voice: Catherine. A laywoman from Siena who wrote and spoke to the pope in Avignon, warmly and without fear, urging him to return to Rome.

carryVoice: Your line: if you are what you should be. Warm, honest, and unafraid of power. Catch you tomorrow.
